reader: AI reader 22 (targeted check at the stated place, web full texts)
source_read: All three web full texts read in the app's browser in tabs of my own: huang_2022, PMC10231478 (first tab, before the browser bridge dropped; its Table 3 cell checked again in the second tab); tanz_2025, https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/74/wr/mm7432a1.htm, and dean_2018, PMC6006320 (second tab, after the bridge came back). Paragraphs counted as the locator convention says; heading structure checked in each page.

results.note: Every value matches at the stated places. 37 not seeking treatment and 41 controls; 6.9 days of abstinence with urine negative on testing days (Participants 1st paragraph). Grades before self-reported first use (Academic records; Table 1 note). GPA 2.1 (0.7) vs 2.5 (0.6) and p = 0.016 (Table 1; Group comparisons 2nd paragraph). Age 34.0 vs 33.7, education 12.6 vs 12.7, estimated IQ 104.9 vs 105.0 (Table 1; the non-significance is stated in Group comparisons 1st paragraph). Model on age, parental income, smoking status and GPA with R2 0.41, d 0.61, t(36) = 3.732, p = 0.001 (Predictive modeling 2nd paragraph). Attention 0.69, p < 0.001; memory 0.46, p < 0.01; executive p = 0.87 (3rd paragraph). Editors' check recomputed: 3.732, 4.177 and 2.805 over sqrt(37) give 0.614, 0.687 and 0.461. The anchor rightly does not cite the executive d, whose printed -0.27 does not fit its t (card reporting issue 2). Role qualifies: right.

corrected.extracted: Scores were standardized to the control group, not to published norms. The shortfall remained with withdrawal partialled out (d 0.54, p = 0.002), with standardized school test scores in place of grades (24 and 19 participants; d 1.41) and in grade-matched subgroups of 28 (d 0.71). Lifetime alcohol, cocaine, marijuana and other drug abuse or dependence: 26, 12, 21 and 9 of 37 in the methamphetamine group vs 9, 0, 9 and 0 of 41 controls. The authors state that effects of methamphetamine are difficult to disentangle from other drug use (their data cannot tell whether this leads to under- or overestimation), that the methods do not show a causal relationship, that the predictors explain about 40% of the variance, and that the control sample was modest for prediction.

results.note: Numbers confirmed. Standardized to controls rather than published norms (Cognitive battery). d 0.54, t(36) = 3.302, p = 0.002 (Predictive modeling 4th paragraph). d 1.41, t(23) = 6.888, in the subset with test scores, 24 and 19 per Academic records and the Table 1 note (6th paragraph). 28 per group, d 0.71 (7th paragraph). Lifetime diagnoses 9/26, 0/12, 9/21, 0/9 (Table 1). Not causal, about 40% of variance, modest control sample (Discussion 7th paragraph). One wording correction: Discussion 4th paragraph says it is 'difficult to disentangle' methamphetamine from other substance use; 'cannot' applies only to telling the direction of the resulting bias with these data. Role qualifies: right.

corrected.locator: Methods › Study population, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Findings, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 2, All row

results.note: Every number matches at the stated places: 74,601 and 298,404 (Findings 1st paragraph; also Study population 2nd paragraph); 1,722 / 367,696 / 4.68 and 1,144 / 1,487,536 / 0.77, crude 6.08 (5.64 to 6.55), adjusted 5.28 (4.90 to 5.70) (Table 2 All row; Findings 2nd paragraph); 3.75% vs 0.63% at the end of 10 years (Findings 2nd paragraph). Study population 1st paragraph gives the linkage, ages 18 or older, the urine tests, first arrest as index date, comparisons insured in the index year and four per exposed person frequency matched on index year, age and sex. Only one element sits outside the stated locator: the 1st paragraph excludes earlier psychosis for the comparisons only; the exclusion for all subjects, both cohorts, is in the 2nd paragraph, hence the locator correction. The adjustment set (age, sex, comorbidities) is in Findings 2nd paragraph and Table 2 footnote. The 10-year figures are Kaplan-Meier estimates with death treated as censoring. Role supports: right for an association claim (same direction).

corrected.extracted: The 23 substances defining exposure include methamphetamine, amphetamine, MDMA and MDA; no breakdown by substance is given. Adjustment: age, sex and five comorbidity diagnoses (depression, anxiety, ischaemic heart disease, cardiovascular disease, stroke) recorded at any time during 2007–2016; nothing for other drug or alcohol use, socio-economic position or family history. Outcome codes listed: 295, 296.04, 296.14, 296.24, 296.34, 296.44, 296.54 and 296.64 (mood disorders with psychotic features), 297, 298.0, 298.1, 298.4, 298.8, 298.9 and 780.1; the drug-induced psychosis codes 292.1, 292.11 and 292.12 appear only in the exclusion list, although the text says other stimulant use disorders with psychosis were included. The authors state that the analysis was not preregistered and should be considered exploratory.

results.note: All content is at the stated places: 23 substance names counted in Study population 1st paragraph (methamphetamine, amphetamine, MDMA and MDA among them; no breakdown anywhere); comorbidities diagnosed during 2007-2016 (3rd paragraph) and the adjustment set (Table 2 footnote †); the code lists and the included-diagnosis list naming other stimulant use disorders with psychosis (2nd paragraph); not preregistered, exploratory (Data source 2nd paragraph). The only change is precision: the anchor wrote '296.04–296.64', which reads as a range of all codes from 296.04 to 296.64 (including mood-disorder codes without psychotic features); the paper lists seven codes, each ending in 4, and the correction lists them. Role qualifies: right.

corrected.extracted: By number of arrests, counted from the index date to the end of the study, adjusted HRs: one 4.49 (4.09–4.93), two 5.07, three 5.24, four 5.53, five or more 6.25 (5.42–7.20); p for trend 0.038, printed in the incidence-rate column, which a linear regression of the five category rates on the number of arrests reproduces (editors' calculation). Person-years per person rise from about 4.4 with one arrest to 6.5 with five or more (editors' calculation). The authors state that the database has no validated measures of dose, frequency, amount or severity, so dose dependence could not be asserted, that arrests reflect police activity and priorities and do not capture all use (many people who use are never arrested), that the comparison group may include people who use amphetamines, and that people who use more often may be more likely to be arrested.

results.note: Numbers confirmed against Table 3 (4.49, 4.09 to 4.93; 5.07; 5.24; 5.53; 6.25, 5.42 to 7.20) and Findings 4th paragraph. The p for trend 0.038 sits in the fifth cell of its row, the IR column, checked in the page's table cells. Arrests counted from the index date to the study end date (Statistics 1st paragraph). Editors' calculations recomputed: the regression of 4.40, 4.80, 4.81, 4.84 and 5.45 on 1 to 5 gives t = 3.56, df 3, p = 0.0377; with the zero category p = 0.070, and on log HRs p = 0.004, so only the five-rate regression reproduces the printed value. Person-years per person: 178,802/40,880 = 4.37 and 42,589/6,572 = 6.48. Conclusions 3rd paragraph (no validated measures of dose, frequency, amount or severity) and 6th paragraph (police activity, comparison group may include people who use, more frequent use more likely arrested) match. One correction: the authors do not say arrests 'miss most use'; they say arrests do not capture all use and many people who use will never be detected or arrested. Role qualifies: right.

corrected.locator: Methods › Data Sources, 1st paragraph; Results › SUDORS: Stimulant-Involved Overdose Deaths During January 2021–June 2024, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table, Overall (49 states and DC) row, methamphetamine columns; main-text footnotes §§ and †††
corrected.extracted: SUDORS, January 2021–June 2024, 49 states and DC (jurisdictions had to report at least 75% of their overdose deaths in at least one 6-month period; California and Wisconsin were included for part of the period, Texas and Wyoming only for January–June 2024, North Dakota not included): of 309,274 unintentional or undetermined-intent overdose deaths, 96,614 (31.2%) involved methamphetamine, meaning that the medical examiner or coroner listed it as a cause of death on the death certificate, in their report or in the postmortem toxicology report; 66,475 (68.8% of these; 21.5% of all deaths) also involved opioids and 30,139 (9.7% of all deaths) did not. Any stimulant: 182,502 (59.0%), 73.0% of them with opioids.

results.note: Every number confirmed (Table Overall row: 309,274; 96,614 (31.2%); 66,475 (21.5%); 30,139 (9.7%); 182,502 (59.0%). Results SUDORS 1st paragraph: 68.8% and 73.0%; 2nd paragraph: 182,502). Shares recomputed: 66,475/96,614 = 68.8%, 30,139/309,274 = 9.75%. Three corrections. (1) Footnote §§ defines involvement as listed 'as cause of death'; the anchor dropped that, which reads like detection. (2) Footnote ††† states the rule as at least 75% in at least one 6-month period; the anchor's 'included for 6-month periods in which they reported at least 75%' is an inference. (3) Locator: the symbols are the main-text footnotes. The Table reuses §§ and ††† for other content (the circumstance-data rule; history of stimulant use) and gives these two rules as its footnotes * and §. The unintentional or undetermined intent scope is in Data Sources 1st paragraph, now added. Role supports: right.

Data Sources 2nd paragraph (X40-44, Y10-14; T43.6 'which primarily includes methamphetamine and other amphetamines'). Main-text footnote ¶¶ (2000 US Census Bureau standard population; the ¶¶ mark sits in Statistical Analysis 2nd paragraph). Results > NVSS 1st paragraph (psychostimulants 3.9 to 10.4; cocaine 4.5 to 8.6). Introduction 1st paragraph (2,266 in 2011 and 34,855 in 2023, cited to NCHS Data Brief 522; provisional 2024 declines without figures). All match. Wording note: the paper says 'Across groups, the largest increases were in deaths co-involving stimulants and opioids'; 'in every racial and ethnic group' is a fair reading. The statement concerns stimulants as a whole (cocaine and psychostimulants), not T43.6 alone. Role supports: right.

corrected.extracted: Among methamphetamine-involved deaths with circumstance data (46 states and DC; 67,831 deaths), those without opioids more often had a known history of cardiovascular disease (hypertension excluded; 39.3% vs 19.8%) and were more often seen in an emergency department for the fatal overdose (30.3% vs 17.4%), and less often had evidence of opioid use (12.2% vs 41.1%). Among all methamphetamine-involved deaths (49 states and DC), those without opioids were older (aged 45–54, 55–64 and 65 or older: 27.1%, 27.9% and 9.2% vs 21.3%, 14.3% and 3.2%). The authors expect stimulant-involved deaths to be underestimated: some are certified with cardiovascular causes and get no overdose code, and postmortem toxicology varies and does not routinely test for emerging stimulants.

results.note: Every number confirmed against the Table, methamphetamine columns. Circumstance N 67,831 (46,985 with and 20,846 without opioids). Cardiovascular 9,288 (19.8) and 8,200 (39.3), with Table footnote *** (hypertension excluded). Seen in ED 7,989 (17.4) and 6,244 (30.3). History of opioid use 19,333 (41.1) and 2,543 (12.2). Ages 14,147 (21.3), 9,498 (14.3), 2,125 (3.2) with opioids and 8,176 (27.1), 8,400 (27.9), 2,774 (9.2) without. Limitations paragraph (first and second limitations; 'underestimation'); Results SUDORS 3rd paragraph (46 states and DC; methamphetamine patterns comparable). One correction: the age rows sit in the Table's Overall section (all 96,614 methamphetamine-involved deaths, 49 states and DC), not among deaths with circumstance data, so the corrected text gives the age contrast its own population. Note that the contrasts are crude (no age standardization). Role qualifies: right.
